  "text": "Tobias Reel came down from the church when the bell had done. The light was ordinary. There were gulls.\n\nHe took the beach road because it was the way home and for no other reason, and he counted the posts as he had counted them for forty years, and there were eleven, and the tide was where the almanac said it ought to be. The sand below the house was smooth. No footprints up, no footprints down. The sea had been over it and taken its time.\n\nThe house was dark. He saw that from the dune. The door was shut. He went up the twenty steps and stood on the porch and did not knock, because post eleven had been there before him and he did not care to follow it.\n\nThrough the front window the room was as a room is when no one has been in it since evening. The lamp stood on the sill. He could see the chip in the base. He could see it had not been lit; there was no smut on the glass, and the wick was white.\n\nThe rug was damp. He could tell by the colour. A dark patch, the shape of a slope.\n\nHe went back down the path. At the lantern he stopped and set it right, since it had slipped on its hook, and it rang once, and he waited, and it did not ring again.\n\nWhen the village asked, he said she had gone up the hill. It was what you said.",

He walked the twenty steps and looked through the front window and came down again. The lamp stayed on the sill. The rug stayed where it was. By December the dark patch had gone, or had become the colour of the rest, which he supposed was the same thing.\n\nIn January a boy from the Carrows' place came running to say there was a light in Maren's window. Tobias put on his coat. From the dune he could see it, low and yellow and steady, the way a lamp is when it has been trimmed by someone who knows the lamp.\n\nHe went up. He stood on the porch. Through the glass the lamp was lit, and the wick was black, and the chip in the base was there, and the chair by the window was pushed back from the sill as if someone had risen from it a moment before.\n\nHe did not knock.\n\nHe went down the path and set the lantern right, though it had not slipped, and it did not ring at all, and he waited a long time to be sure of that.\n\nHe told the boy it was the moon on the glass.   "text": "The lamp burned through February. Tobias went up on Sundays and on other days too, and it was always lit, and the oil never went lower in the glass. He did not ask himself who filled it. There are questions a man can carry up a path and questions he cannot, and he had learned which were which.\n\nIn March the thaw came off the hill and the beach road ran with it. He walked the eleven posts in water to the ankle and counted them, and there were eleven, and he was ashamed of how glad that made him.\n\nOn the porch he smelled the stove.\n\nNot smoke. The smell a stove has when it has been warm all night and let go out in the morning: iron and ash and something underneath like bread. His mother's kitchen had smelled like it. Maren's mother's kitchen had smelled like it, forty years ago, when he brought the fish up and was given tea.\n\nHe put his hand flat on the door. The wood was warm. Only the wood, and only where his hand was, and he stood with it there until he could not tell whether the warmth was the door's or his own.\n\nHe did not knock. He did not try the latch.\n\nGoing down he did not look at the lantern. He heard it, though, once, small and clear behind him, and he did not turn, because turning is also a kind of knocking.\n\nAt the Carrows' they asked. He said the sea was high. It was what you said.",
